title: Hoisting
concept: JavaScript pulls variable and function declarations to the top of their scope (hoisting)

steps.title: Global Variable Declaration
steps.explanation:
`var message = 'Hello'` executes.
var has **function scope** and is hoisted.
steps.keyInsight: Before running your code, the JS engine pulls all var declarations to the top of their scope.

steps.title: Call the greet() Function
steps.explanation:
Call the `greet()` function.
A function scope is created and the var declarations inside the function are **hoisted**.
steps.keyInsight: When a function is called, all var variables inside it are first initialized to undefined.

steps.title: Verify Hoisting — Output undefined
steps.explanation:
`console.log(inner)` executes.
inner hasn't been assigned yet, but thanks to **hoisting**, it outputs `undefined` without an error.
steps.keyInsight: var hoists only the declaration; the assignment runs at its original location. That's why it's undefined!
steps.analogy: It's like putting a name tag 'inner' on a desk first (declaration), then putting contents in later (assignment).

steps.title: Execute the Actual Assignment
steps.explanation:
The assignment part of `var inner = 'World'` executes.
Now inner = 'World'.
steps.keyInsight: Hoisting only lifts the declaration. The assignment (= 'World') runs at its original location.

steps.title: Check the Value After Assignment
steps.keyInsight: The same variable has different values depending on where in the code you access it. That's the hoisting trap!

steps.title: Return the Result
steps.keyInsight: message comes from the global scope, inner comes from the function scope (scope chain).

steps.title: Assign to result
steps.explanation: 'Hello World' returned by greet() is stored in the result variable.

steps.title: Print the Final Result
steps.keyInsight: Because of hoisting, the first console.log printed undefined, and the second printed 'World'.

quiz.explanation:
The declaration of var x is hoisted to the top of the function and initialized to undefined.
The assignment (= 10) runs at its original position, so the first console.log prints undefined.

misconceptions.wrong: Hoisting physically moves code to the top of the file
misconceptions.correct:
The code doesn't actually move.
The JS engine simply processes declarations first before executing.
misconceptions.why:
During the compilation phase, declarations are registered in memory. During the execution phase, assignments are performed.
The code itself doesn't change.

misconceptions.wrong: let and const are hoisted just like var
misconceptions.correct: let/const are also hoisted, but the TDZ (Temporal Dead Zone) causes an error if you access them before their declaration.
misconceptions.why:
Accessing let/const before their declaration throws a ReferenceError.
This is a key difference from var.

keyTakeaway: var: only the declaration is hoisted (undefined), assignment runs at original location. let/const: TDZ causes an error on access before declaration.
